thread_title: Sarracenia blood moon revisited and remixed!
breadcrumb: Sarracenia blood moon revisited and remixed!

posts.body_html:
For those of you who aren't familiar with this unofficial cultivar, Sarracenia blood moon is a cross between flava rubricorpora and leucophylla wilkerson's red rocket. The rubricorpora clone used is unknown, presumably a liberty Co, FL genotype. Given that multiple different seedlings from this cross were distributed, we can infer that blood moon is a "grex cultivar," meaning any rubricorpora x wilkerson's red rocket that "looks decent" can be called blood moon.

Challenge with this is, even in the same cross, not all seedlings look exactly alike. Here's arguably the most coveted of the blood moon clones, this is grown and photographed by mbfmark of the Sarracenia forum:



Now here's the blood moon clone grown and photographed by my homie Bristol:


To the discerning grower, both plants are exceptional, but in my opinion, MBFMark's plant is far superior in shape and overall look, as it resembles wilkerson's red rocket shape-wise yet has the rubricorpora colors! When you think of acquiring blood moon, my gut says most growers are probably going to hope to get MBFMARK's clone.

This is exactly the reason why grex cultivars can cause serious trouble: even though the two plants are similar and are siblings from the same cross, they're not equal. Giving clonal names to each individual gets rid of this potential issue. Another solution is to call them by their cross name instead of giving the entire cross a cultivar name. That way, the person acquiring the plant knows it's a variable seedling that fits certain criteria rather than an exact plant that they were eyeball effing (pardon my french). BTW, that's not necessarily a bad thing: if you're like Mike Wang and you grow out hundreds of seedlings that are selected down to a few dozen, you can expect every last one of those individuals to be nice!


Another question one may have is what clone of rubricorpora did the original breeder use to create blood moon? You might wonder, does it even make a difference? Turns out yes, it does!

Ever since Bristol enlightened me of the different blood moon clones in circulation, I've been on a mission to see if I can make a nice plant using a similar cross. I crossed wilkerson's red rocket with flava var. rubricorpora 'best clone' Liberty Co, FL. There's a lot of variability in the offspring, and I started off with close to 1000 seedlings. Recently, I got them down to about 60 or 70 plants, but more culling is necessary to get down to only the best.

It's still a bit early to tell, but here's one I have my eye on, looks different from the two clones above:




Lots of variability in the seed batch, here's another seedling that has nice color, but check out the various colors of it siblings:


it's still too early to tell if any of these will make the cut, but I thought this discussion is important to bring up. to be continued....

The plant in your photo is the same clone that I have Bristol. I got mine directly from Brooks and it is the one that I prefer also. It's the clone that I believe most people would recognize as Blood Moon when they see it. I'm not a fan of the whole grex thing. I feel that if a well known clone has a distinctive look to it a different grex clone, even if it looks similar should not be called the same name. As nice as that clone looks, it is does not look like what is commonly known as Blood Moon. This makes me think of that Leah Wilkerson thread awhile back. JMHO

posts.body_html: So where’s the line between grex  and “imposter “ clones?   I understand  Alucard and Schnell’s Ghost are grex, has Blood Moon joined the list?  Is there a list of legitimate grex somewhere?
posts.body_text: So where’s the line between grex  and “imposter “ clones?   I understand  Alucard and Schnell’s Ghost are grex, has Blood Moon joined the list?  Is there a list of legitimate grex somewhere?

posts.body_html: Imposter clones are typically selfings or look-alikes to registered cultivars that are defined as being clone only. Blood moon isn't a registered cultivar, but since multiple different clones were released, this implies it's a grex cultivar.

posts.body_html:
I'll play. I remade Blood Moon in 2016 using Wilkerson's Red Rocket and an extremely large, dark rubricorpora which has been Phil F's clone of choice for years. The plants were on the tall side last year but nothing crazy, but this year they have come up absolutely gigantic compared to all the other 2016 plants. They are approximately 1.5 times the height of anything else and are beefy to boot. The wooden crossbar on the raccoon cage is 24" above the soil. These traps are just opening now so I'll be back with an update once they harden off and color up.
Untitled by Calen Hall, on Flickr

posts.body_html:
I was lucky few to get my hands on this particular clone from MBFMark (Mark R.), who originally got it from Brooks Garcia, so presumably this may have been the "original" Blood Moon clone when it was published, but who knows. A bit of background on my plant - I received it in early summer 2017 with 2 nice spring pitchers, the plant put up some smaller/spindly fall pitchers that year and no fall pitchers. I repotted it that winter into a larger container with a peat mix and in 2018 got nothing but wimpy pitchers with some nice chunky phyllodia.

This spring it put most of its energy into blooming and I wasn't wise enough to trim some of the buds, it put up only one strong spring pitcher that was devoured by caterpillars. All of this led me to believe Blood Moon was simply a spring pitchering plant due to its rubricorpa heritage. Man, am I glad to be WRONG! Not sure how these will compare with a fully established spring crop, they're not especially tall, but this is the first of at least five nice fall ones coloring up over the past few days.

Fresh opening


After 1 day


Today (2 days after) - still some coloring up to do
